subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: A block hangs from a vertical spring and oscillates up and down. Which statement is correct about the instant at which the block is at its equilibrium position?
options: The block is at rest for an instant, since it is in equilibrium there.
The net force on the block is zero, although the block is moving.
The spring is at its natural length, so it exerts no force on the block.
The net force on the block is largest there, as its speed is largest there.
optionWhy: A student who thinks equilibrium means being at rest picks this. Equilibrium means zero net force. The block is momentarily at rest at the top and bottom of its motion, where the net force is largest.

By definition, the equilibrium position is where the net force is zero: the spring force balances the weight. An oscillating block is not at rest there; it moves through it, and that is where its speed is greatest.

A student who thinks the equilibrium position is where the spring is unstretched picks this. At the natural length the only force on the block is its weight, so the net force is mg. At equilibrium the spring is stretched by mg/k.

A student who thinks the force is largest where the speed is largest picks this. The block's speed is largest at equilibrium, but the net force there is zero; the net force is largest at the turning points.
questions.explain: By definition, the equilibrium position is where the net force is zero: the spring force balances the weight. An oscillating block is not at rest there; it moves through it, and that is where its speed is greatest.

questions.q: A small block slides without friction back and forth across the bottom of a V-shaped trough. Each side of the trough is a straight incline at the same angle θ to the horizontal, and the block passes smoothly from one side to the other at the bottom. The block repeats the same motion in equal intervals of time. Which claim about the block's motion is correct?
options: It is SHM, as any motion that repeats in equal time intervals is SHM.
It is SHM, since the net force on it points back toward the bottom at all times.
It is periodic but not SHM: along each side the net force has a constant magnitude.
It is periodic but not SHM: the constant force along each side keeps its speed constant.
optionWhy: A student who thinks every periodic motion is SHM picks this. Repeating in equal time intervals makes the motion periodic; SHM is the special case in which the restoring force is proportional to the displacement, which is not true here, since the force along each side is mg sin θ at every point.

A student who thinks any force directed back toward equilibrium produces SHM picks this. The force does point toward the bottom, but it has the same magnitude, mg sin θ, at every point on a side; SHM also needs the magnitude to be proportional to the displacement.

On either side the net force on the block is the component of its weight along the incline, mg sin θ, directed down the slope toward the bottom; the normal force cancels the other component. That force has the same magnitude whether the block is near the bottom or far up the side, so it is not proportional to the displacement from the bottom. The motion repeats, so it is periodic, but it is not SHM.

A student who thinks a constant force produces a constant speed picks this. The net force mg sin θ along each side gives the block a constant acceleration, g sin θ, so its speed changes steadily; the motion is not SHM because that force is not proportional to the displacement, not because the speed is constant.
questions.explain: On either side the net force on the block is the component of its weight along the incline, mg sin θ, directed down the slope toward the bottom; the normal force cancels the other component. That force has the same magnitude whether the block is near the bottom or far up the side, so it is not proportional to the displacement from the bottom. The motion repeats, so it is periodic, but it is not SHM.

questions.q: Each of the four graphs shows the net force F exerted on an object as a function of the object's position x along a straight line. Which graph shows a force that would make the object undergo simple harmonic motion about x = 0?
optionWhy: A student who thinks the magnitude of the force only has to be proportional to the displacement, whatever its direction, picks the straight line with positive slope. That force points the same way as the displacement and pushes the object farther from x = 0, so the object does not oscillate about x = 0 at all.

A student who thinks any restoring force that grows with displacement gives SHM picks the curve that steepens away from x = 0. That force is opposite to the displacement, but doubling x more than doubles it, so it is not proportional to x and the oscillation is not SHM.

A student who thinks a restoring force of constant magnitude produces SHM picks the pair of horizontal segments. That force always points back toward x = 0, but it has the same size at every distance, so it is not proportional to the displacement.

The straight line through the origin with negative slope is F = −kx: the force is proportional to the displacement from x = 0 and opposite to it, so it is a restoring force of the kind that produces SHM about x = 0.
questions.explain: The straight line through the origin with negative slope is F = −kx: the force is proportional to the displacement from x = 0 and opposite to it, so it is a restoring force of the kind that produces SHM about x = 0.
questions.working: SHM about x = 0 needs F = −kx with k > 0: a straight line through the origin with negative slope. The positive-slope line pushes the object away from x = 0; the constant-magnitude force and the steepening curve point back toward x = 0 but are not proportional to x.

questions.q: A block of mass 0.50 kg hangs at rest from a vertical spring of spring constant 50 N/m. The block is pulled down a further 0.040 m and released from rest. What is the magnitude of the net force on the block immediately after it is released? Use g = 10 m/s².
optionWhy: A student who measures Δx from the spring's natural length picks this: (50 N/m)(0.14 m) = 7.0 N. That is the spring force alone; the block's weight of 5.0 N acts in the opposite direction, so the net force is 2.0 N.

At equilibrium the spring is stretched 0.10 m, where kΔx balances mg. Pulled 0.040 m lower, the spring force is (50)(0.14) = 7.0 N up and the weight is 5.0 N down, so the net force is 2.0 N up: k times the displacement from equilibrium, (50)(0.040) = 2.0 N.

A student who measures the displacement from equilibrium and then also subtracts the weight picks this: |(50)(0.040) − 5.0| = 3.0 N. Measuring from the equilibrium position already includes gravity, so counting the weight again is a double count.

A student who thinks an object at rest has no net force on it picks this. The block is at rest only for an instant; it is 0.040 m from equilibrium, so the net force on it is k(0.040 m) = 2.0 N toward equilibrium.
questions.explain: At equilibrium the spring is stretched 0.10 m, where kΔx balances mg. Pulled 0.040 m lower, the spring force is (50)(0.14) = 7.0 N up and the weight is 5.0 N down, so the net force is 2.0 N up: k times the displacement from equilibrium, (50)(0.040) = 2.0 N.
questions.working: At the equilibrium position the spring is stretched by mg/k = (0.50 kg)(10 m/s²)/(50 N/m) = 0.10 m. Just after release the stretch is 0.10 m + 0.040 m = 0.14 m, so the spring force is (50 N/m)(0.14 m) = 7.0 N upward, and the weight is (0.50 kg)(10 m/s²) = 5.0 N downward. Net force = 7.0 N − 5.0 N = 2.0 N upward. Equivalently, F = k × (displacement from equilibrium) = (50 N/m)(0.040 m) = 2.0 N.

questions.q: A block hanging from a vertical ideal spring oscillates with period T_E on Earth. The same block and spring are taken to the Moon, where the gravitational field is weaker, and the block is set oscillating vertically. How does the period on the Moon compare with T_E?
options: It is the same: g shifts the equilibrium position but does not alter m or k.
It is longer: weaker gravity adds less to the spring's restoring force there.
It is the same: like a pendulum's period, it does not depend on g at all.
It is shorter: the block has less mass on the Moon, so it oscillates more quickly.
optionWhy: The period of an object–spring oscillator is T_s = 2π√(m/k). On the Moon the block's weight is smaller, so the spring stretches less at equilibrium, but m and k are unchanged and the period is T_E.

A student who thinks gravity adds to the restoring force of a vertical oscillator picks this. Gravity is constant, so it shifts the equilibrium position; the net force about that position is still −k times the displacement.

A student who thinks a pendulum's period depends only on its length, and so is the same on any planet, picks this. The claim about the spring is right, but the reason is wrong: a pendulum's period, 2π√(l/g), does depend on g. The spring's period is unchanged because T_s = 2π√(m/k) contains neither g nor anything that g alters.
A student who confuses mass with weight picks this. The block weighs less on the Moon, but its mass, which sets its inertia in T_s = 2π√(m/k), is the same everywhere.
questions.explain: The period of an object–spring oscillator is T_s = 2π√(m/k). On the Moon the block's weight is smaller, so the spring stretches less at equilibrium, but m and k are unchanged and the period is T_E.

questions.q: The graph shows the position x of an object in simple harmonic motion as a function of time t. What is the angular frequency ω of the motion?
optionWhy: A student who treats angular frequency as the same as frequency picks this: f = 1/(0.50 s) = 2.00 Hz. Each cycle is 2π rad, so ω = 2πf = 12.6 rad/s.
The curve returns to its maximum, 0.10 m, every 0.50 s, so T = 0.50 s. Then ω = 2π/T = 2π/(0.50 s) = 12.6 rad/s.
A student who uses the period in place of the frequency picks this: ω = 2π(0.50) = 3.14. The frequency is the reciprocal of the period, 2.0 Hz, so ω = 2π(2.0 Hz) = 12.6 rad/s.
A student who reads the period as the time from a maximum to the next minimum, 0.25 s, picks this: 2π/0.25 = 25.1 rad/s. That is half a cycle; the motion repeats completely only after 0.50 s.
questions.explain: The curve returns to its maximum, 0.10 m, every 0.50 s, so T = 0.50 s. Then ω = 2π/T = 2π/(0.50 s) = 12.6 rad/s.
questions.working: The motion repeats completely (x = 0.10 m, at rest, about to move in the negative direction) at t = 0, 0.50 s and 1.00 s, so T = 0.50 s. ω = 2π/T = 2π/(0.50 s) = 12.6 rad/s. (Equivalently f = 1/T = 2.0 Hz and ω = 2πf.)

figure.alt: Graph of position x (m) against time t (s) from t = 0 to 1.00 s. The vertical axis is marked 0.10, 0 and −0.10; the time axis is marked 0.25, 0.50, 0.75 and 1.00, with dashed vertical gridlines at those times. The curve is a smooth cosine-shaped oscillation that starts at x = 0.10 m at t = 0, crosses zero at 0.125 s, reaches −0.10 m at 0.25 s, crosses zero again at 0.375 s, returns to 0.10 m at 0.50 s, and repeats the same pattern, ending at 0.10 m at 1.00 s.

questions.q: A block attached to a horizontal ideal spring oscillates on a frictionless surface with period T₀. The block is replaced by a block with nine times the mass, attached to the same spring. What is the new period?
optionWhy: A student who takes the period to be proportional to the mass picks this. The period depends on the square root of the mass, so it increases by a factor of √9 = 3.
A student who recalls the period as 2π√(k/m) picks this: the period would fall by a factor of 3. A heavier block accelerates less for the same spring force, so its period is longer: T_s = 2π√(m/k).
T_s = 2π√(m/k), so with the same spring the period is proportional to √m. Nine times the mass gives √9 = 3 times the period.

A student who thinks the period of a mass–spring oscillator does not depend on the mass, as a pendulum's does not, picks this. The spring force does not grow with the mass, so the heavier block oscillates more slowly.
questions.explain: T_s = 2π√(m/k), so with the same spring the period is proportional to √m. Nine times the mass gives √9 = 3 times the period.
questions.working: T_s = 2π√(m/k). With k unchanged, T ∝ √m, so T_new/T₀ = √(9m/m) = 3. New period = 3.00T₀.

questions.q: A 0.50 kg block attached to an ideal spring of spring constant 200 N/m oscillates on a frictionless horizontal surface. What is the frequency of the oscillation?
optionWhy: A student who gives the period's value as the frequency picks this. 0.31 s is the period; the frequency is 1/(0.31 s) = 3.2 Hz.
A student who treats angular frequency as frequency picks this: √(k/m) = √(200/0.50) = 20 rad/s is ω. The frequency is ω/(2π) = 3.2 Hz.
A student who recalls the period as 2π√(k/m) gets T = 2π(20) = 126 s and f = 0.0080 Hz. The period is 2π√(m/k) = 0.31 s, so f = 3.2 Hz.

questions.q: An object in SHM oscillates about x = 0 with amplitude A. Which statement correctly describes the object at the instant it is at x = +A?
options: Its velocity is zero, and its acceleration has its greatest magnitude, toward −x.
Its velocity is zero, and so its acceleration is zero at that instant too.
Its velocity is zero, and its acceleration is greatest in magnitude, toward +x.
Its velocity and its acceleration both have their greatest values, toward +x.
optionWhy: At a turning point the object is momentarily at rest. Its displacement has its greatest magnitude, so a = −ω²x has its greatest magnitude, Aω², and points toward equilibrium, the −x direction.

A student who thinks an object at rest has no acceleration picks this. The velocity is zero for an instant, but it is changing from +x to −x; the restoring force, and so the acceleration, is largest at x = +A.
A student who thinks the acceleration points along the displacement picks this. The size is right, but a = −ω²x points toward equilibrium: toward −x when x = +A.
A student who thinks x, v and a peak together picks this. At x = +A the velocity is zero, a quarter cycle out of step with x, and the acceleration points toward −x.
questions.explain: At a turning point the object is momentarily at rest. Its displacement has its greatest magnitude, so a = −ω²x has its greatest magnitude, Aω², and points toward equilibrium, the −x direction.

questions.q: An object oscillates in SHM about x = 0 with amplitude A. Point P is at x = 0, point Q is at x = +A/2 and point R is at x = +A. Which ranks the magnitude of the object's acceleration at P, Q and R?
optionWhy: A student who thinks the acceleration is largest where the object moves fastest picks this. Speed ranks P > Q > R, but the acceleration depends on position: it is zero at P, where the speed is greatest.
A student who thinks the acceleration has the same magnitude throughout SHM picks this. a = −ω²x varies with position: zero at equilibrium, greatest at the turning points.

A student who thinks zero velocity means zero acceleration sets the acceleration to zero at R, where the object is momentarily at rest, as well as at P. At R the acceleration is in fact the largest of the three.
|a| = ω²|x|, so the acceleration is proportional to the distance from equilibrium: ω²A at R, ω²A/2 at Q and zero at P.
questions.explain: |a| = ω²|x|, so the acceleration is proportional to the distance from equilibrium: ω²A at R, ω²A/2 at Q and zero at P.
questions.working: |a| = ω²|x|: at P, 0; at Q, ω²A/2; at R, ω²A. So R > Q > P.

questions.q: Which of the following describes resonance in an oscillating system?
options: The natural frequency shifting until it matches the driving force's frequency
A large increase in amplitude that occurs whenever the driving force is strong
A large increase in amplitude when a periodic force acts at the natural frequency
Oscillation that keeps going at the natural frequency after the driving force stops
optionWhy: A student who thinks a driving force changes the system's own frequency picks this. The natural frequency is set by the system (for a spring, k and m); resonance happens when the driving frequency matches it.

A student who thinks only the size of the driving force matters picks this. A strong force at a frequency far from the natural frequency gives only a small amplitude; the frequency match is what produces resonance.
Resonance is the growth of the amplitude to a large value when a periodic (sinusoidal) external force is exerted at the system's natural frequency.

A student who uses 'resonate' in its everyday sense of continuing to ring picks this. Free oscillation after the force stops is not resonance, which is the large amplitude produced while the force acts.
questions.explain: Resonance is the growth of the amplitude to a large value when a periodic (sinusoidal) external force is exerted at the system's natural frequency.

questions.q: A block attached to an ideal spring on a horizontal frictionless surface oscillates with a period of 2.2 s when released from rest 3.0 cm from equilibrium. The block is then released from rest 6.0 cm from equilibrium. What is the new period?
optionWhy: A student who thinks the block takes twice as long because it travels twice as far picks this. It also moves twice as fast, because the restoring force at corresponding points of the cycle (for example, at the turning points) is doubled.
The period of an object on a spring, T_s = 2π√(m/k), does not depend on the amplitude. With the same block and spring, the period stays 2.2 s.
A student who thinks the larger restoring force returns the block sooner picks this. The larger force is matched by the larger distance, so the period is unchanged.

A student who treats the motion as constant acceleration of the same size as before, t = √(2d/a), picks this: √2 × 2.2 s. In SHM the acceleration is not constant; it scales with the amplitude, so the time does not change.
questions.explain: The period of an object on a spring, T_s = 2π√(m/k), does not depend on the amplitude. With the same block and spring, the period stays 2.2 s.
questions.working: For SHM the period, T_s = 2π√(m/k), does not depend on the amplitude. Doubling the amplitude from 3.0 cm to 6.0 cm leaves T = 2.2 s.

questions.q: A block attached to an ideal horizontal spring oscillates in SHM on a frictionless surface. Which of the following is the total mechanical energy of the block–spring system at any instant?
options: The block's kinetic energy plus the spring's potential energy at that same instant
The block's maximum kinetic energy plus the spring's maximum elastic potential energy
The block's kinetic energy at that instant only, as only the block has mass
The kinetic energy plus the potential energy plus the work done by the spring
optionWhy: Mechanical energy is the sum of the system's kinetic and potential energies at the same instant: E_total = U + K, where K is the block's and U is the spring's.
A student who adds the two maxima picks this. They occur at different places and each equals the total energy, so their sum is twice the total.
A student who leaves the spring out of the system picks this. The stretched or compressed spring stores elastic potential energy, which is part of the system's mechanical energy.
A student who counts the spring's work in addition to its potential energy picks this. The potential energy already accounts for the spring force inside the system; adding the work counts it twice.
questions.explain: Mechanical energy is the sum of the system's kinetic and potential energies at the same instant: E_total = U + K, where K is the block's and U is the spring's.

questions.q: A block attached to an ideal spring oscillates in SHM on a horizontal frictionless surface with amplitude A. Take x to be positive when the spring is stretched. Where is the elastic potential energy of the system at its maximum?
options: At x = +A only, since the spring has negative energy when compressed
At x = +A and at x = −A, where the block's kinetic energy is zero
At x = 0, where the kinetic energy of the block is also at its maximum
At every position equally, since mechanical energy is conserved
optionWhy: A student who thinks a compressed spring stores negative energy picks this. U = (1/2)k(Δx)² is the same for a compression or a stretch of the same size.
U = (1/2)kx² is largest where |x| is largest, at both turning points, where the block is momentarily at rest and K = 0.
A student who thinks K and U peak together picks this. At x = 0 the spring is relaxed, so U = 0, and all the energy is kinetic.
A student who thinks conservation keeps each form constant picks this. Only U + K is constant; U changes with position as (1/2)kx².
questions.explain: U = (1/2)kx² is largest where |x| is largest, at both turning points, where the block is momentarily at rest and K = 0.

questions.q: A block on an ideal spring oscillates in SHM with angular frequency ω on a horizontal frictionless surface. When the block is a distance d from equilibrium, its speed is v. What is the block's maximum speed?
optionWhy: A student who treats kinetic energy as proportional to speed writes (1/2)mv_max = (1/2)mv + (1/2)mω²d² and picks this. K = (1/2)mv², so the squares of the speeds add.
Conservation of energy: (1/2)mv² + (1/2)kd² = (1/2)m v_max². With k = mω², this gives v_max² = v² + ω²d².

A student who takes the present position d as the amplitude, ignoring the block's kinetic energy there, picks this: v_max = Aω with A = d. The block is moving at x = d, so its amplitude is larger than d.
A student who thinks the block moves at the same speed everywhere picks this. The speed increases as the block approaches equilibrium, where U is least and K is greatest.
questions.explain: Conservation of energy: (1/2)mv² + (1/2)kd² = (1/2)m v_max². With k = mω², this gives v_max² = v² + ω²d².
questions.working: Energy is conserved: (1/2)mv² + (1/2)kd² = (1/2)m v_max². With k = mω²: v_max² = v² + ω²d², v_max = √(v² + ω²d²).

questions.q: The diagram shows a block on a horizontal frictionless surface attached to an ideal spring. The block oscillates in SHM between the positions marked −A and +A. Which ranks the block's kinetic energy at the positions marked P, Q and R?
optionWhy: A student who thinks K and U are largest at the same places picks this. U is larger at Q and R than at P, so K, which equals E − U, is smaller there.
A student who thinks conservation keeps the kinetic energy constant picks this. Only K + U is constant; K is largest where U is smallest, at P.
K = E_total − (1/2)kx². At P, x = 0, so U = 0 and K = E. Q and R are the same distance A/2 from equilibrium, so U = E/4 and K = 3E/4 at both.
A student who thinks a compressed spring has negative potential energy gives R (compressed side) the most kinetic energy. U = (1/2)k(Δx)² is the same for a compression or a stretch of A/2.
questions.explain: K = E_total − (1/2)kx². At P, x = 0, so U = 0 and K = E. Q and R are the same distance A/2 from equilibrium, so U = E/4 and K = 3E/4 at both.
questions.working: K = E − (1/2)kx². P (x = 0): K = E. Q (x = +A/2) and R (x = −A/2): U = E/4, K = 3E/4 each. So P > Q = R.

questions.q: The diagram shows a uniform rod swinging with small amplitude as a physical pendulum about a fixed horizontal axis through its upper end. Points P and Q are marked on the rod. How does the period T_Q of the motion of point Q compare with the period T_P of the motion of point P?
optionWhy: A student who treats each point as a separate simple pendulum of its own length, with T ∝ √ℓ, picks this: Q is twice as far from the axis as P, giving √2 times the period. The points are joined rigidly, so they cannot swing independently; they share one period.

A student who thinks the time for a cycle grows with the distance traveled picks this: Q's arc is twice as long as P's. Q also moves twice as fast as P, so both points complete a cycle in the same time.

The rod is rigid, so every point on it turns through the same angle θ(t) at the same time. P and Q therefore return to their starting positions together, and the whole rod has a single period. Q moves along a longer arc than P, but at a proportionally greater speed.

A student who thinks points farther from the axis rotate faster picks this: Q's speed is twice P's. Q's greater linear speed comes from its greater distance from the axis; both points have the same angular velocity and the same period.
questions.explain: The rod is rigid, so every point on it turns through the same angle θ(t) at the same time. P and Q therefore return to their starting positions together, and the whole rod has a single period. Q moves along a longer arc than P, but at a proportionally greater speed.
questions.working: The rod is rigid, so θ(t) is the same for every point. A point at distance r from the axis is displaced along an arc rθ and moves with speed r|dθ/dt|, but it returns to its starting position whenever θ does. Hence T_Q = T_P (= 2π√(I/(mgd)) for the rod).

questions.q: For small oscillations, the small-angle approximation and Newton's second law in rotational form give the following equation for a physical pendulum: d²θ/dt² = −ω²θ. Which statement correctly describes the quantity ω in this equation?
options: It is the angular velocity, dθ/dt, which changes as the pendulum swings.
It is the angular frequency, 2π/T, which is greater for larger amplitudes.
It is the angular frequency, 2π/T, which stays constant throughout the motion.
It is the frequency, 1/T, which is the number of oscillations completed each second.
optionWhy: A student who reads ω with its meaning from rotational kinematics picks this. The pendulum's angular velocity dθ/dt does change, from zero at the turning points to a maximum at equilibrium, but the ω in the SHM equation is the constant angular frequency √(mgd/I).

A student who thinks larger swings return sooner, so that ω increases with amplitude, picks this. ω² = mgd/I depends only on the pendulum, not on the amplitude, within the small-angle approximation that gives this equation.
ω is the angular frequency of the oscillation. Comparing Iα = −mgdθ with d²θ/dt² = −ω²θ gives ω² = mgd/I, which is fixed by the pendulum, so ω is constant; T = 2π/ω.
A student who treats angular frequency and frequency as the same quantity picks this. The frequency is f = 1/T, in hertz; the angular frequency is ω = 2πf = 2π/T, in radians per second.
questions.explain: ω is the angular frequency of the oscillation. Comparing Iα = −mgdθ with d²θ/dt² = −ω²θ gives ω² = mgd/I, which is fixed by the pendulum, so ω is constant; T = 2π/ω.
questions.working: Newton's second law in rotational form with sin θ ≈ θ: I d²θ/dt² = −mgdθ, so d²θ/dt² = −(mgd/I)θ. Comparing with d²θ/dt² = −ω²θ: ω² = mgd/I, a constant fixed by the pendulum's mass, rotational inertia and center-of-mass distance. ω is the angular frequency, T = 2π/ω, f = ω/(2π); the angular velocity dθ/dt = −θ₀ω sin(ωt + φ) varies.

questions.q: A torsion pendulum consists of a horizontal uniform disk suspended from a vertical wire attached to its center. The disk undergoes small rotational oscillations about the wire, for which Iα = −kΔθ. Which single change would increase the period of the oscillations?
options: Replacing the disk with a thin ring of equal mass and radius
Twisting the disk through a larger angle before it is released
Taking the apparatus to a location where the value of g is smaller
Replacing the disk with a heavier one of the same rotational inertia
optionWhy: The period is T = 2π√(I/k). A thin ring has all its mass at the radius R, so its rotational inertia, MR², is twice that of a uniform disk of the same mass and radius, (1/2)MR². The period becomes √2 times as long.

A student who thinks a wider swing takes longer because the disk turns farther picks this. The restoring torque is proportional to the angle, so a larger amplitude gives proportionally larger angular speeds and the period, 2π√(I/k), is unchanged.
A student who thinks gravity provides the restoring torque, as for a simple pendulum, picks this. The torque comes from the twisted wire, so T = 2π√(I/k) does not depend on g.

A student who treats the torsion pendulum like a block on a spring, with T = 2π√(m/k), picks this. For rotational oscillations the inertial quantity is the rotational inertia; with I unchanged, the period is unchanged.
questions.explain: The period is T = 2π√(I/k). A thin ring has all its mass at the radius R, so its rotational inertia, MR², is twice that of a uniform disk of the same mass and radius, (1/2)MR². The period becomes √2 times as long.

questions.q: A uniform disk of radius R = 0.10 m hangs from a fixed horizontal axle that passes through a point on its rim, perpendicular to the face of the disk. The rotational inertia of a uniform disk of mass M about an axis through its center, perpendicular to its face, is (1/2)MR². The disk is displaced through a small angle and released. What is the period of its oscillations? Use g = 10 m/s².
optionWhy: The axle is a distance d = R from the center of mass, so by the parallel axis theorem I = (1/2)MR² + MR² = (3/2)MR². Then T = 2π√(I/(Mgd)) = 2π√((3/2)R/g) = 2π√(0.015 s²) ≈ 0.77 s.

A student who uses the rotational inertia about the disk's center, (1/2)MR², gets 2π√(R/(2g)) ≈ 0.44 s. The disk rotates about the axle on its rim, so its rotational inertia about that axle, (3/2)MR², must be used.

A student who models the disk as a point mass at its center, a distance R from the axle, gets 2π√(R/g) ≈ 0.63 s. The disk's mass is spread out, so its rotational inertia about the axle is (3/2)MR², not MR².

A student who treats the disk as a simple pendulum whose length runs from the axle to the bottom of the disk, ℓ = 2R, gets 2π√(2R/g) ≈ 0.89 s. The disk is not a point mass; its period is 2π√(I/(Mgd)) with d = R.
questions.explain: The axle is a distance d = R from the center of mass, so by the parallel axis theorem I = (1/2)MR² + MR² = (3/2)MR². Then T = 2π√(I/(Mgd)) = 2π√((3/2)R/g) = 2π√(0.015 s²) ≈ 0.77 s.
